messages.subject: Simple Multivariate Normal Question
parts:
Hi,

I have what I think is a relatively simple question about modeling multivariate normal data.  My data consists of N independent d-dimensional multivariate normals, (assume d is small, like 2, but N possibly large).  They all have the same covariance but different means.  

What is the best way to implement this efficiently, with vectorization?  Since N is large I want to do this as efficiently as possible.

Should I represent my data as an N x 2 matrix, and then doing something like

for(idx in 1:N){ 
      y[idx,] ~ multi_normal(mu[idx,],Sigma)
}

I had read that the sampling statements in loops are relatively slow, so I was thinking there should be a way to represent this using some sort of reparameterization:

z ~ normal(0,1)
y <- mu+L*z

where z is a Nx2matrix as well, but its not clear to me that this is possible when y is data and not a transformed parameter.

Also, mu is of much smaller effective dimension than N (like in regression), so I'd prefer not to represent mu as a transformed parameter.  I think my problem is somewhat similar to the multivariate regression example in the manual, but my outcome is multivariate as well.

Thanks for any insight!

messages.subject: Re: Simple Multivariate Normal Question
parts:
On Friday, May 30, 2014 11:05:23 AM UTC-4, Alexander Franks wrote:
I have what I think is a relatively simple question about modeling multivariate normal data.  My data consists of N independent d-dimensional multivariate normals, (assume d is small, like 2, but N possibly large).  They all have the same covariance but different means.  

What is the best way to implement this efficiently, with vectorization?  Since N is large I want to do this as efficiently as possible.

Should I represent my data as an N x 2 matrix, and then doing something like

for(idx in 1:N){ 
      y[idx,] ~ multi_normal(mu[idx,],Sigma)
}

The most efficient way to access K-variate data by "rows" is to use an N-array of K vectors (or possibly row_vectors but not in this case). Like

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
  int<lower=1> N;
  vector[K] y[N];
}

then you can loop over that

for(idx in 1:N) {
  y[idx] ~ multi_normal(mu[idx], Sigma);
}

where mu is has the same structure. However, if K = 2, then it would probably be faster to use increment_log_prob and your own coding of a bivariate normal without matrix algebra.

I had read that the sampling statements in loops are relatively slow, so I was thinking there should be a way to represent this using some sort of reparameterization:

z ~ normal(0,1)
y <- mu+L*z

where z is a Nx2matrix as well, but its not clear to me that this is possible when y is data and not a transformed parameter.
Right, that is for the case where y is an unknown.

Also, mu is of much smaller effective dimension than N (like in regression), so I'd prefer not to represent mu as a transformed parameter.  I think my problem is somewhat similar to the multivariate regression example in the manual, but my outcome is multivariate as well.

If the issue is simply that you do not want to store the samples of mu, then you can construct mu in the model block rather than the transformed parameter block.

Ben
